title: Trail running and outdoor fitness
subtitle: Forest trail notes, a muddy hill run, views on outdoor exercise, the history of trail running, and a local running club

parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Trail note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Lucas,

I wanted to tell you about my first weekend with the local trail running group. I was worried that I might not [1] up with the faster runners, so I joined the steady-pace group on Saturday morning. Our leader reminded everyone to [2] attention to tree roots and loose stones on the steep forest path. Halfway up the ridge, we stopped at a wooden shelter, [3] gave us a chance to catch our breath and drink some water. You do not need to own expensive gear to start, because any pair of sturdy shoes will [4] well on dry tracks. Let me know if you feel like coming [5] with us next Sunday!

Best,
Gemma

questions.explanation: 'Keep up with' is a phrasal verb meaning to move at the same speed as others; 'hold' and 'stay' do not form this phrasal verb.
'Pay attention to' is a fixed collocation meaning to watch or listen carefully; 'give' and 'make' do not collocate with 'attention to'.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause referring to the whole action of stopping at the shelter.
'Work well' means function effectively in this context; 'act' and 'serve' do not fit naturally with 'shoes' on a track.
'Come along' means to join someone in an activity or go somewhere with them.

parts.title: Text cohesion: First hill race
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: At eight o'clock on Sunday morning, I stood near the wooden gate at the bottom of Pine Hill, waiting for my first ten-kilometre trail race to begin. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: Once we reached the grassy summit, the cool breeze cooled my face and I could see the whole valley below.
When the whistle finally blew, around eighty runners set off slowly along a narrow, muddy path between the trees.
At the bottom, a volunteer handed me a warm cup of tea and a shiny wooden medal to remember the morning.
After the first two kilometres, the route turned sharply uphill and everyone had to walk over wet stones.
From that high point, the return path was wide and dry, so I ran steadily all the way back to the gate.

gaps.explanation: 'When the whistle finally blew' follows directly from waiting for the race to begin at the bottom of the hill.
'After the first two kilometres' continues the progress along the muddy path and introduces the steep uphill climb.
'Once we reached the grassy summit' completes the uphill climb mentioned in the previous sentence.
'From that high point' refers back to the grassy summit and describes running down the return path to the gate.
'At the bottom' follows running back to the gate and closes the story with the volunteer handing out tea and a medal.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Outdoor fitness
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about trail running and exercising outdoors. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Aisha
texts.text: I used to pay for an expensive city gym, but running on indoor treadmills always felt boring. Moving my workouts to local forest trails saved me money and made exercise something I actually look forward to. Because the ground changes every few metres, my mind stays busy watching for roots and puddles. I prefer heading out alone early in the morning before work, as the quiet paths help me plan my day.

texts.title: Kieran
texts.text: People often assume you need to buy expensive GPS watches and special waterproof jackets before you can enjoy trail running. Honestly, I think a basic pair of gripping shoes and an old T-shirt are enough for most local parks. What really matters to me is the social side. I joined a Saturday morning fitness group last spring, and chatting with other members makes even a rainy five-kilometre jog feel much shorter.

texts.title: Holly
texts.text: Living in a flat with no garden, I rely on outdoor fitness parks and hill paths to get fresh air after sitting at a desk all day. In winter, though, dark afternoons and icy pavements make outdoor running tricky. When the weather turns freezing, I switch to indoor swimming rather than risking a twisted ankle on slippery mud. I also wish local councils would put clearer distance signs along popular woodland routes.

texts.title: Omar
texts.text: I started trail running after injuring my knee on hard city pavements two years ago. Running on soft grass and earth is much gentler on my joints, and I have not had any pain since I made the change. Unlike road races where everyone stares at their watches, trail runners rarely care about finishing times. Most people I meet on the hills are happy to slow down and enjoy the scenery.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Running off the road
parts.instructions: Read the article about the growth of trail running and outdoor fitness. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Long before smooth asphalt roads and running tracks existed, running across hills and fields was simply a practical part of rural life. Shepherds, messengers, and villagers regularly jogged along narrow dirt paths to carry news or check on animals before nightfall. In several mountainous regions, friendly local races over steep slopes became popular at summer festivals during the nineteenth century. At that time, nobody called the activity trail running; it was simply moving quickly across the countryside.

During the 1970s, a major running boom swept through large cities, and millions of people bought cushioned trainers to jog on flat pavements and park lanes. While road running grew rapidly, a smaller group of runners began leaving busy streets behind to explore forest tracks and coastal cliffs. They preferred quiet natural paths over traffic noise and hard concrete. By the 1990s, outdoor sports companies noticed this trend and started designing lighter shoes with deeper rubber grips for mud and rock.

Moving from flat pavements onto uneven earth changes how the body works. On a smooth road, every step lands in almost the exact same way, which can tire out the same muscles and joints. On a forest trail, however, runners constantly adjust their stride length to step over roots, balance on slanted stones, and climb short slopes. Fitness coaches point out that this variety strengthens ankles, hips, and core muscles while also improving everyday balance.

Physical benefits are only half the story, as many outdoor runners say their main reason for heading into the hills is mental rest. Spending forty minutes under green trees or beside an open river helps lower stress after a long day indoors. Unlike a crowded gym with bright screens and loud music, a natural trail offers changing seasons, bird calls, and fresh air. Even a short walk-and-jog session in a local wood can leave people feeling calmer.

At the same time, outdoor fitness requires sensible preparation because weather and light can change quickly away from town centres. A sunny valley can turn cold and windy at the top of a ridge, and a dry path can become slippery after twenty minutes of rain. Experienced club leaders always remind newcomers to check the forecast, carry a charged phone, and tell someone which route they plan to follow before setting off alone.

As trail running has become more popular, national parks and local charities have noticed extra wear on fragile paths. When dozens of runners step off a muddy track to keep their shoes clean, the path slowly widens and damages nearby plants. To protect the countryside, many running clubs now teach simple trail manners: stay on the marked route even through puddles, carry all snack wrappers home, and step aside politely for walkers and cyclists.

In many towns, outdoor fitness is no longer just for competitive athletes chasing fast times. Community groups now organise relaxed weekly sessions that welcome beginners, families, and older adults who want to stay active together. Some groups combine slow jogging with bodyweight exercises on park benches, while others meet for Saturday morning hill walks followed by coffee. By focusing on enjoyment rather than speed, these clubs help more people build lasting healthy habits.

headings: How varied terrain builds different muscles
Simple habits to protect natural paths
Choosing the right waterproof jacket for winter
Why nature helps runners clear their minds
Staying safe when conditions shift outdoors
Early countryside running before modern roads
Inclusive groups make outdoor exercise social
City joggers spark demand for off-road gear

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes how shepherds, messengers, and villagers ran along dirt paths and held local hill races long before modern roads.
Paragraph 2 explains how runners leaving city pavements for trails led sports companies to design specialised off-road shoes.
Paragraph 3 explains how stepping over roots, stones, and slopes strengthens ankles, hips, and core muscles.
Paragraph 4 focuses on how exercising among trees and fresh air lowers stress and offers mental rest.
Paragraph 5 warns about sudden weather changes on ridges and advises checking forecasts, carrying a phone, and sharing routes.
Paragraph 6 describes trail manners such as staying on marked paths, taking litter home, and giving way to protect fragile nature.
Paragraph 7 explains how community groups welcome beginners and families for social jogs, park exercises, and coffee.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a park ranger about creating a new fitness trail (questions 1-2), then a runner about returning to outdoor sport after an injury (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Lucas, a park ranger, talking about building a new three-kilometre fitness trail in Oakwood Park.

turns.speaker: lucas
turns.text: When the town council asked my team to design a new three-kilometre fitness trail in Oakwood Park, most visitors assumed we would pour a wide concrete path right through the middle of the woods. That is usually the cheapest option to maintain. However, concrete changes how rainwater drains and damages tree roots, so we chose crushed gravel instead, following old footpaths that were already there. That way, runners get a firm surface without harming the woodland. I expected the Saturday running clubs to use the loop right away, and they certainly did. What really surprised me, though, was seeing so many office workers from nearby streets walking the trail in their trainers during lunch breaks. Even better, local dog walkers have started helping us clear fallen branches after windy nights. Seeing different groups share one natural space politely has been the best result of the whole project.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Holly, an amateur runner, talking about returning to trail running after hurting her ankle.

turns.speaker: holly
turns.text: Two summers ago, I twisted my ankle badly on a rocky hill path and could not run for four months. When the doctor finally said I could start moving outdoors again, I imagined I would be back to running ten kilometres within a couple of weeks. In reality, rebuilding my confidence was much harder than rebuilding my fitness. Every small stone on the path made me nervous about falling again. What helped me most wasn't buying stronger ankle supports or following a strict training chart — it was joining a slow beginner group where nobody cared about speed. Walking the steep bits together and chatting took my mind off my foot. Whenever friends ask how to recover from a sports injury, I tell them not to rush back to their old distances too soon. Start with short, flat routes on dry days, celebrate small steps, and give your body plenty of time to trust the trail again.

parts.title: Compare two photographs
parts.instructions: Look at the two photographs. First describe and compare them (45 seconds), then answer the two numbered questions (45 seconds each).
parts.prompt:
Tell me what you see in these two photographs and compare the two ways of keeping fit. Then answer these two questions:
1. What are the advantages of exercising outdoors in a park compared with training indoors at a gym?
2. Which of these two activities would you prefer to do on a weekend morning, and why?

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you did an outdoor physical challenge or long walk. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a time when you walked, ran, or exercised outdoors for longer than usual.
2. How did you feel during the activity and after you finished?
3. Why do you think spending time being active in nature is important for people today?
